name: Interview brainteasers, set 2
description: Interview brainteasers: hourglasses, common knowledge, pigeonholes, loops of boxes, last digits, growth, speeds, rates and board colourings. Each item keeps its own schedule.

items.prose: You have a 5-minute and an 8-minute hourglass, with all their sand at the bottom. Each time you turn a glass over counts as one turn, the turns that start them included. Timing starts at your first turn.
items.question: What is the fewest turns that times exactly 11 minutes?

widget.accept: 4: start both, turn the 5 when it runs out, and turn it again when the 8 runs out.
widget.label: Turns

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Look at what the 5-minute glass holds when the 8 runs out.

byKey.starts-free: You did not count the turns that start the two glasses. They count, so the plan takes four.
byKey.one-start: You counted one turn to start both glasses. Each glass needs its own turn.

explain.text: Start both, and turn the 5 again when it runs out at 5 minutes. When the 8 runs out at 8 minutes, the 5 has run 3 minutes since its turn. Turn it over: those 3 minutes run back, ending at 11.

items.prose: Five logicians each have a mark on the forehead or none. Each sees the others but not their own. Three are marked. A host says: "At least one of you is marked." Each round, all say at once whether they know their own mark.
items.question: In which round do the marked logicians first say they know?

options.text: Round 3: two silent rounds rule out one mark and two marks.
Round 1, since each marked logician sees two marks.
options.why: Seeing two marks tells you nothing about your own. If you are clean, those two could be all.

options.text: Round 5, one round for each logician.
options.why: You counted every logician. The rounds follow the marks: three marks, three rounds.

options.text: Never, since everyone already sees a mark, so the host adds nothing.
options.why: Each saw a mark, but nobody knew that everyone knew it. The host makes it common knowledge.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask what would happen with one mark, then with two.

explain.text: With one mark, its owner sees none and knows in round 1. With two, each sees one and knows in round 2, once round 1 is silent. So with three, the marked logicians know in round 3, and the other two in round 4.

items.prose: Twenty-five people are in a room. Take each birthday to fall in one of the 12 months.
items.question: What is the largest number of people you can be sure share one birth month?

options.why: Two is certain, but so is more. Twelve months hold only 24 people at two each, so the 25th makes three.
You took 12 from 25. The people can spread out evenly, so only three in a month is certain.

options.text: None, since months differ in length.
options.why: Month lengths do not matter here. Twelve boxes and 25 people force a box of three.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Spread the people over the months as evenly as you can.

explain.text: Twelve months can hold 24 people at two each, with no month of three. The 25th person must make three in some month. So $\lceil 25/12 \rceil = 3$ is the most you can be sure of.

items.prose: A drawer holds socks in five colours, with plenty of each. You take socks out in the dark, one at a time.
items.question: How many must you take to be sure of four socks of one colour?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Play the unluckiest drawer: how many socks can you take with no four alike?

byKey.pairs: That is the count for a pair. For four alike, each colour can hide three socks first.
byKey.all: You took four of every colour. You need four of just one.
byKey.no-plus-one: Fifteen socks can be three of each colour. One more sock forces four.

explain.text: The unluckiest draw takes three of each colour, 5 × 3 = 15 socks, with no four alike. The next sock must make four of some colour. So 16 socks are enough, and 15 are not.

items.prose: A hundred prisoners each have a number. The numbers lie shuffled in 100 boxes, one per box. Each prisoner may open 70 boxes. He starts at the box with his own number, then opens the box named by each number he finds.
items.question: Roughly what is the chance that every prisoner finds his number?

options.text: About 65%: all succeed exactly when no loop is longer than 70.
About 0%: each succeeds 70% of the time, so $0.7^{100}$.
options.why: You treated the prisoners as independent. Following the numbers ties their fates to the same loops.

options.text: About 70%: each prisoner succeeds 70% of the time.
options.why: That is one prisoner's chance. The team needs every loop to be 70 or shorter.

options.text: About 35%: one long loop is the only way to fail.
options.why: About 0.35 is the chance of a loop over 70, which is failure. Take it from 1.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A prisoner fails exactly when his loop is longer than 70.

explain.text: A loop of length $k > 70$ appears with chance $1/k$, and at most one can. So failure has chance $\tfrac{1}{71} + \dots + \tfrac{1}{100} \approx 0.35$. Success is about 1 − 0.35 = 0.65.

items.question: What is the last digit of $17^{2031}$?

widget.accept: 3: powers of 7 end 7, 9, 3, 1 in turn, and 2031 = 4 × 507 + 3.
widget.label: Last digit

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Only the last digit, 7, matters. Find the cycle of its powers.

byKey.r1: You took the first entry of the cycle. 2031 leaves remainder 3 on division by 4, so take the third.
byKey.r2: You used remainder 2. 2031 = 4 × 507 + 3, so take the third entry of the cycle.
byKey.r0: You treated 2031 as a multiple of 4. It leaves remainder 3.

explain.text: Only the last digit matters, so look at powers of 7: they end 7, 9, 3, 1 and repeat. 2031 = 4 × 507 + 3, so the third entry applies. The last digit is 3.

items.prose: A balance grows at 6% a year, compounded yearly.
items.question: About how many years does it take to triple, to the nearest year?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Compare tripling with doubling, or take logs.

byKey.doubling: That is the doubling time, 72/6. Tripling takes about 1.6 doublings.
byKey.quadruple: That is two doublings, a fourfold rise. Tripling needs about 1.6 doublings.
byKey.simple: You used simple interest, 200% ÷ 6%. Compounding gets there sooner.

explain.text: Tripling takes ln 3 / ln 1.06 years. With ln 3 ≈ 1.099 and ln 1.06 ≈ 0.058, that is about 18.9. Or take 1.6 doublings of 12 years each, about 19.

items.prose: A courier drives 63 miles to a depot at 30 mph. She drives the same road back at 70 mph.
items.question: What is the average speed for the round trip, in mph?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the total distance by the total time.

byKey.mean: You averaged the two speeds. The slow leg takes longer, so it counts for more.
byKey.one-way: You divided one leg's 63 miles by the whole 3 hours. The round trip is 126 miles.

explain.text: Out takes 63/30 = 2.1 hours and back takes 63/70 = 0.9 hours. That is 126 miles in 3 hours. So the average is 126/3 = 42 mph.

items.prose: Three pumps can each fill a tank alone. The first takes 6 hours, the second 8 and the third 12. Only the first two are switched on.
items.question: How many hours do they take to fill the empty tank? Give two decimal places.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the fractions of the tank each pump fills in an hour.

byKey.average: You averaged 6 and 8 hours. Two pumps together are faster than either alone.
byKey.all-three: You switched on all three pumps. Only the first two run.
byKey.sum: You added the times. Add the rates instead: 1/6 + 1/8 of a tank an hour.

explain.text: The first pump fills 1/6 of the tank an hour and the second 1/8. Together that is 7/24 of a tank an hour. So they take 24/7 ≈ 3.43 hours.

items.prose: A 10 by 10 board loses two opposite corner squares. Each domino covers two squares that share an edge.
items.question: Can 49 dominoes cover the 98 squares that remain?

options.text: No. Both corners have one colour, so the colours are 48 and 50.
Yes, since 98 squares is exactly 49 dominoes of two squares.
options.why: You checked the area only. Each domino covers one dark and one light square, and the colour counts differ.

options.text: Yes, if the dominoes run round the board in a spiral to the centre.
options.why: You hoped a clever layout would work, but none can. Each domino covers one square of each colour, so 49 of them need 49 of each.

options.text: No, because 98 is not a multiple of 4, so the dominoes cannot pair up.
options.why: You asked for a multiple of 4, but a domino covers 2 squares, so 98 is fine. The barrier is the colour count, not the area.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Colour the board like a chessboard and count each colour.

explain.text: Opposite corners of an even board share a colour. Removing them leaves 48 squares of that colour and 50 of the other. Every domino covers one of each, so 49 dominoes would need 49 of each.
